clues.clue: An allowance Roman soldiers received for buying salt evolved into this word for regular pay.
Anatomists named this tissue from the Latin for 'little mouse' — one seems to scurry when you flex.
Plague-wary Venice made ships wait 40 days, a span whose Italian name gives us this isolation term.
Now a detective's lead, this word was once spelled 'clew' and meant a ball of thread like the one Theseus followed.
From Latin 'nescius,' meaning ignorant, this bland little compliment meant 'foolish' in the Middle Ages.
A messenger's fabled run from a Greek battlefield to Athens gave this 26.2-mile race its name.
The name of this sturdy blue-jean twill contracts 'serge de Nimes,' after its French hometown.
This formal dinner jacket owes its name to a tony 1880s club colony in New York's Ramapo Mountains.
Louis Reard named this two-piece of 1946 for a Pacific atoll where the U.S. had just tested an atomic bomb.
Mineral springs in a Belgian Ardennes town lent every steamy resort this 3-letter word.
Robin Williams urges his 'Dead Poets Society' students to heed this 2-word Horace motto: 'seize the day.'
Latin for 'you shall have the body,' this writ forces the state to bring a prisoner before a judge.
Latin for 'it does not follow,' this term tags a reply with no logical link to what came before.
Literally 'without which not,' this 3-word phrase denotes an absolutely indispensable element.
Cicero loved to pose this 2-word question, 'to whom is it a benefit?', to expose who profits from a crime.
Greek roots meaning 'love of wisdom' built this word for the discipline of Plato and Kant.
Greek for 'river horse,' it's the barrel-shaped African mammal that spends its days submerged.
From the Greek for 'flesh-eater,' this stone coffin's limestone was reputed to consume the corpse inside.
Moliere titled a comedy for this character type whose Greek name means 'hater of humankind.'
Greek 'stone' plus the ichor of the gods: this 1964 coinage names the earthy scent of rain on dry soil.
'I've told you a billion times' commits this figure of wild, deliberate exaggeration.
Calling a firing a 'workforce adjustment' deploys this figure that trades blunt words for gentle ones.
When 'the crown' means the monarchy and 'the press' means journalists, this substitution device is at work.
Churchill's 'we shall fight on the beaches' speech pounds away with this device of repeated openings.
Greek for 'yoking,' it's the device letting one verb pull double duty: 'she stole his heart and his wallet.'
This punctuation mark turns 'cannot' into 'can't' and hands the cat ownership of 'the cat's pajamas.'
'Seeing is believing' opens and closes with this -ing verb form that does a noun's job.
Star Trek's 'to boldly go' famously commits this grammatical sin by wedging an adverb mid-verb.
'If I were a rich man' fiddles with this verb mood reserved for wishes and contrary-to-fact musings.
Latin for 'more than perfect,' it's the tense at work in 'she had already left.'
Born as British university slang in the 1890s, this portmanteau meal pairs midmorning eggs with mimosas.
Blending 'motor' and 'hotel,' this roadside lodging boomed along Route 66.
Coined around 1905 for London's pea-soup air, this blend packs smoke and fog into one grimy syllable.
An 1812 cartoon spotted a salamander in a district drawn under Massachusetts Gov. Elbridge Gerry, hatching this political verb.
In 'Through the Looking-Glass,' Lewis Carroll fused 'chuckle' and 'snort' into this gleeful verb.
Thomas More minted this word for an ideal commonwealth from Greek meaning 'no place.'
Karel Capek's 1920 play 'R.U.R.' introduced this word for artificial workers, from the Czech for drudgery.
Milton coined this name for the capital of Hell in 'Paradise Lost'; today it means sheer uproar.
After a tale of three princes from old Sri Lanka, Horace Walpole coined this word for happy accidents in 1754.
This word for a studious square first appeared as a creature's name in Dr. Seuss' 1950 'If I Ran the Zoo.'
County Mayo tenants ostracized their English land agent in 1880, turning his surname into this shunning tactic.
A skinflint French finance minister's surname stuck to this cheap shadow-profile style of portrait.
Ballet dancers owe the name of this skin-tight one-piece to a French trapeze star of the 1860s.
A German physician whose 'animal magnetism' seances entranced 1780s Paris left us this verb for captivating.
A British officer's 1780s exploding case shot put his surname on this word for flying shell fragments.
Thanks to Dickens' 1843 miser, any tightwad risks being branded with this humbugging surname.
Cervantes' windmill-tilting knight lives on in this adjective for gallantly impractical idealism.
An aunt in Sheridan's 'The Rivals' praises 'the very pineapple of politeness'; her name gives us this term for such slips.
Playing the 'glad game' through Eleanor H. Porter's 1913 novel, this heroine became a byword for sunny optimism.
The hypnotist who molds the singer Trilby in an 1894 novel became this term for a manipulative mastermind.
German handed English this word for the guilty thrill of watching a rival slip on a banana peel.
Candles, wool socks & cocoa embody this Danish word for cozy contentment that fueled a 2010s lifestyle craze.
Fado singers steep in this Portuguese word for a bittersweet longing for what's lost or far away.
This Japanese aesthetic term savors imperfection and impermanence, like a tea bowl mended with gold.
Desmond Tutu championed this Nguni word, roughly 'I am because we are'; it also names a Linux system.
Japanese for 'empty orchestra,' this bar-night pastime invites anyone to butcher a power ballad.
In Swahili this word means any journey; English reserves it for expeditions after the Big Five.
Yiddish for a clumsy oaf — literally a 'wooden block' — this word fits anyone who trips over air.
A Hindu deity whose colossal temple chariot rolls through Puri, India gave us this word for an unstoppable force.
American troops in the Philippines borrowed Tagalog's word for 'mountain' to name this remote back country.
